the topographical and temporal aspects of event-related potentials.

the N400 is a complex phenomenon that can be decomposed into several distinct components.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the N400 is not a single unitary process, but a complex of multiple processes, which are not necessarily related to each other, and which can be distinguished by topographical mapping.
the N400 is a complex phenomenon that can be described in terms of multiple microstates that are not necessarily related to a single underlying mechanism.
we have shown that there is no single N400, but multiple distinct N400s, which can not arise from modulation of a single map, but are due to multiple different patterns of neural activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
event-related potential maps are not invariant, but can vary systematically across conditions.
microstates of brain activity are not a single pattern of brain activity, but a set of patterns that differ in topography, and in the strength of the gradient of activity across the cortex.
the N400 can be decomposed into distinct microstates that differ in topography and gradient strength, and that these microstates are sensitive to the surface form of words.
